title: Shark Teeth Found in the Desert!
summary:
Imagine standing in a hot, dusty desert. Now imagine that same spot covered by a warm, shallow sea full of sharks. That's what Egypt's Western Desert looked like 70 to 80 million years ago!

A team of scientists led by Dr. Tarek Yassin from Cairo University made a huge discovery there. They found 14 fossilized shark teeth in dark rocks. A fossil is the leftover shape of a living thing, saved in rock for a very long time.

The teeth came in different shapes. Some were thin and needle-like, perfect for grabbing slippery fish. Others were wide with sharp, jagged edges for slicing. The teeth belonged to five different shark species. Two of them had never been found in Egypt before!

One tooth came from an ancient relative of the goblin shark, a deep-sea shark that still swims today. This might be the first time this species has been found in Africa.

So why are so many teeth in one place? It wasn't a disaster. Over millions of years, sharks lost their teeth, and the teeth sank into the seafloor. The soft ground slowly turned to rock, trapping the teeth inside like a time capsule.

Dr. Yassin says this is probably just one piece of a much bigger story. Who knows what else is buried out there?
why_it_matters: Fossils like these show that even a hot, dusty desert was once a completely different world, and that scientists can rebuild the past from small clues in rocks.

background_read: Cairo University is one of Egypt's biggest and oldest universities, found in the country's capital city, Cairo.
Sharks have been swimming in Earth's oceans for hundreds of millions of years — they appeared long before the dinosaurs did — and a single shark loses thousands of teeth in its lifetime.
Egypt's Western Desert is part of the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world, and its rocks hold fossils of sea animals from the time an ocean covered the land.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists led by Dr. Tarek Yassin from Cairo University
WHAT: They found 14 fossilized shark teeth from five different species in dark rocks — two species never seen in Egypt before
WHERE: In Egypt's Western Desert, which was covered by a warm, shallow sea 70 to 80 million years ago
WHY: Over millions of years, sharks dropped their teeth, the teeth sank into the seafloor, and the soft ground slowly turned to rock that kept them like a time capsule

perspectives.description: They are thrilled because one tooth may be the first of its kind found anywhere in Africa, and the site is probably part of a much bigger story.
They note that 14 teeth from one place is only a small clue, so more digging will be needed to be sure what the ancient sea really looked like.
They see the find as a great example of how deserts were once seas, and how much of Earth's history is still buried and waiting.
